titleEn: Three glasses, one guest: Morocco's mint-tea ritual
facts: Moroccan mint tea, atay, is gunpowder green tea steeped with a fistful of fresh spearmint and sugar; it is served all day, in homes, shops and offices.
The host pours from a height of 30-50 cm to aerate the tea and raise a foam called the crown, a visible mark of skill and care for the guest.
A common saying describes the three glasses served as bitter like life, strong like love and gentle like death; families repeat it without treating it as a rule.
Tea drinking spread in Morocco in the 18th and 19th centuries through Atlantic and Mediterranean trade in green tea, and sugar became a household staple through the same routes.
Refusing a glass can read as refusing hospitality, while asking for a third is a way of honouring the host.
exampleEn: A shopkeeper in Fez pours the first glass from waist height, hands it to the customer before pouring his own, and refills the pot for a second, weaker round.
qualificationEn: The three-glass saying, sugar level and pouring style vary by household and region, and the Sahara version is noticeably sweeter than the coastal one.

titleEn: Lanterns after iftar: Ramadan nights in Cairo
facts: During Ramadan, balconies and shopfronts across Cairo are hung with fanous, lanterns of coloured glass and tin whose patterns glow after sunset.
The custom is popularly traced to the Fatimid period, and one often-repeated story has residents greeting the caliph with lanterns at the start of Ramadan.
Children traditionally carried small lanterns through the streets and sang Ramadan songs such as 'Wahawi ya Wahawi' for sweets and coins.
Metalworkers in neighbourhoods such as Darb al-Ahmar still make lanterns by hand, though cheaper imported electric versions have taken much of the market.
Ramadan reverses the city's clock: streets fill after iftar, shops stay open late and the pre-dawn meal keeps bakeries busy until the call to prayer.
exampleEn: A family hangs a new tin lantern above the entrance before maghrib; the children take a smaller one to the courtyard to sing for neighbours.
qualificationEn: The Fatimid origin story is popular rather than firmly settled history, and lantern styles and street customs differ between Cairo, Alexandria and the countryside.

titleEn: Roasting beans in the front room: Ethiopia's coffee ceremony
facts: The ceremony is led by a woman of the household, who roasts green beans on a flat pan over coals and walks the smoking pan around the room so guests can smell it.
The beans are pounded in a mortar and brewed in a narrow clay pot, the jebena, then poured into small cups in three rounds known as abol, tona and baraka, the last being the blessing.
Fresh grass is spread on the floor and incense burned; the whole sequence can take an hour or more and is a way of honouring visitors rather than a quick drink.
Leaving before the third round is impolite, and the ceremony is used for family talks, reconciliations and community meetings as well as for guests.
Coffee's birthplace is usually placed in the Ethiopian highlands, although the best-known origin story about the goatherd Kaldi is legend rather than record.
exampleEn: A visitor arrives unannounced in Addis Ababa; within twenty minutes the pan is out, the room smells of roasting coffee and the first small cup is passed on a tray.
qualificationEn: Urban offices often shorten the ceremony and some families use electric grinders, while Eritrea shares a closely related ritual with local variations.

titleEn: Your birthday is part of your name: Akan day names
facts: Akan children receive a day name, the kradin, from the weekday of their birth: Kwame for a Saturday-born boy, Ama for a Saturday-born girl, Kwaku for Wednesday, and so on.
The day name is used in everyday address and is also tied in Akan belief to the child's kra, the life force or soul, and to expected character traits.
Many Akan families hold an outdooring ceremony on the eighth day after birth, when the child is brought outside for the first time, named before witnesses and given water and other symbolic tastes.
Most Ghanaians also carry a Christian or Muslim given name, so a full name may combine a European name, a day name and a family name.
Akan names vary between Asante, Fante and Akuapem traditions, and the same weekday has different forms across those groups.
exampleEn: A new colleague introduces himself as Kwabena, and everyone in the office instantly knows he was born on a Tuesday and can greet him with the matching proverb.
qualificationEn: The day-name system belongs to Akan-speaking groups and is not a national Ghanaian custom; other Ghanaian communities follow different naming rules.

titleEn: Know me, know you: how a Yoruba marriage is negotiated
facts: A Yoruba marriage traditionally moves through stages: the introduction, when both families meet and state their intentions, and the engagement, idana, when the bride's family formally accepts the groom.
Between those stages the two families investigate each other's character, health, reputation and background, a process often summarised as knowing the family before marrying the person.
At the engagement the groom's family brings symbolic goods that may include kola nut, bitter kola, honey, salt, fish and a holy book, laid out for the bride's family to inspect and bless.
The groom and his friends prostrate before the bride's parents, and the bride's family offers prayers and advice; the couple often wear aso ebi, matching cloth chosen by each family.
Church or mosque solemnisation and a registry ceremony are usually held separately, so many couples celebrate two or three events on different days.
exampleEn: At an engagement in Ibadan, the groom's cousins kneel with trays of kola and honey while an aunt checks the list and the bride's father gives the final blessing.
qualificationEn: The sequence, the goods and the scale of the event differ between Yoruba subgroups, Muslim and Christian families, and rural and city households.

titleEn: Harambee: who pays when a Kenyan community has a need
facts: Harambee is a Swahili call meaning 'all pull together', and it names both communal work and the fundraising meetings that pay for a need.
Common causes are school fees, funerals, hospital bills, church building and water projects; organisers set a target and invite relatives, colleagues and neighbours.
At a harambee, an MC calls donors by name and announces each amount, producing a public record and a strong social incentive to give.
Jomo Kenyatta promoted the practice after independence in 1963 as a nation-building ethic, and 'harambee' is part of Kenya's national motto.
Scholars and journalists note that public pledging can create pressure on poorer households, and politicians sometimes use harambee to build patronage.
exampleEn: A colleague's father dies and the office WhatsApp group posts a harambee date; on Saturday people gather in a hall, an MC reads names into a microphone and the total is announced at the end.
qualificationEn: Harambee takes very different forms in rural self-help groups, urban offices and political rallies, and not every Kenyan supports the public-pledge model.

titleEn: Umuganda: the last Saturday morning in Rwanda
facts: Umuganda is a community work day held on the last Saturday of each month, officially from 8 to 11 in the morning, when residents clean roads, build houses or plant trees.
Local authorities organise the tasks and participation is officially mandatory; non-attendance can be sanctioned by local officials or raised when residents request certain services.
After the work, neighbours hold a short meeting where officials give information and residents raise local problems.
The word means coming together for a common purpose; the practice draws on older communal work traditions but was formalised as national policy in the 2000s.
It is promoted as one of Rwanda's homegrown solutions for cleanliness, infrastructure and social cohesion, and it is also used to mobilise support for government programmes.
exampleEn: On the last Saturday of the month, a Kigali neighbourhood clears a drainage channel together, then sits on plastic chairs for a meeting about a broken water point.
qualificationEn: Participation is not purely voluntary, and human-rights organisations have criticised enforcement, so it should be described as official policy as well as a social practice.

titleEn: Famadihana: when highland Malagasy families rewrap their dead
facts: Famadihana, the turning over of the bones, is a highland ceremony in which a family opens the tomb, lifts out ancestors' remains and rewraps them in fresh lamba cloth.
It is usually held every five to seven years in the dry season from July to September, and because it is expensive families may postpone it for years.
The wrapped remains are carried and danced with to live music, and the family shares rum and a large meal; the mood is often joyful rather than mournful.
The rite expresses the belief that ancestors, razana, remain involved in the lives of the living and must be honoured and kept informed.
Some Christian churches and health authorities have discouraged the practice, and today it is kept by some Merina and Betsileo families rather than by all Malagasy people.
exampleEn: In a highland village, a family opens the tomb at dawn, lays out new silk lamba, rewraps a grandfather's remains and dances with him to a brass band before returning him to the tomb.
qualificationEn: Famadihana is a living custom among particular highland groups and some families have abandoned it, so it should not be described as a national Malagasy practice.

titleEn: Teranga: what a Senegalese host owes a stranger
facts: Teranga, from Wolof, is the widely shared ideal of Senegalese hospitality: a guest is welcomed, fed and treated as an honour rather than an interruption.
In practice a visitor is offered water or ataya, the strong sweet green tea brewed three times in small glasses and served in rounds that structure conversation.
A common saying gives the three glasses as bitter like death, sweet like life and gentle like love, a proverb repeated across the Sahel with local variations.
The value extends beyond friends: strangers asking directions may be walked to their destination, and sharing a meal with a visitor is expected even in modest households.
Teranga is also a national brand, used in tourism campaigns and in the nickname of the national football team, the Lions of Teranga.
exampleEn: A stranger asks for an address in Dakar; a shopkeeper points, then walks him two streets, and when they arrive the family insists he sit for a glass of ataya.
qualificationEn: Teranga is a normative ideal rather than a description of every encounter, and economic strain, city life and tourism marketing all stretch the practice.

titleEn: The hammam as a weekly appointment
facts: A hammam is a neighbourhood bathhouse with a sequence of cool, warm and hot rooms, and in Tunisia it is used weekly by many men and women, often before Friday prayers or a wedding.
The scrub is a social ritual in itself: black olive-oil soap, a rough kessa glove and a marble slab, sometimes with an attendant doing the exfoliation.
Hammams are spaces for news, advice and preparation; before Eid or a wedding, families book the hot room for hours.
Many historic hammams were endowed as charitable foundations attached to mosques, which is why some of the oldest stand in the medina next to religious buildings.
Home bathrooms, gas costs and water scarcity have closed many hammams, and heritage groups now campaign to keep the remaining ones open.
exampleEn: On a Thursday afternoon in Tunis, a mother and daughter take their buckets and soap to the hammam, spend an hour in the steam and catch up with neighbours on the marble bench.
qualificationEn: Gender, timing and pricing vary by town and family, and the weekly rhythm is a norm rather than a universal habit.

region: Somalia and the Horn of Africa
titleEn: Xeer: Somali custom before there was a state
facts: Xeer is a customary legal system built on agreements between clan groups and on the authority of councils of elders, who hear disputes and cite precedent.
Responsibility is collective: compensation for injury or death is usually paid by the offender's clan group to the victim's, most famously in camels and livestock.
Elders mediate rather than judge, and decisions are enforced through clan pressure, reputation and the threat of reciprocal claims.
The system long predates the modern state and kept functioning after the central government collapsed in 1991, alongside sharia courts and, in the north, formal local government.
It covers grazing and water rights, marriage, injury and homicide, but critics say it can disadvantage women and minority groups who lack equal standing in clan councils.
exampleEn: Two herders from different clans quarrel over a well; elders from both sides meet under a tree, hear witnesses and agree on compensation to be delivered in livestock.
qualificationEn: Xeer is not a single written code: it varies by clan and region and works differently in cities, and it should be described alongside sharia rather than as the only Somali law.

titleEn: Ubuntu: a person is a person through others
facts: Ubuntu is a humanist idea from Nguni languages, usually summarised in the maxim Umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu: a person is a person through other people.
It describes personhood as relational, achieved through community, generosity and mutual recognition rather than through individual autonomy alone.
The concept became a public value after apartheid, invoked by Archbishop Desmond Tutu in the Truth and Reconciliation Commission and later in Constitutional Court judgments on eviction and dignity.
The root -ntu means person and the prefix u- signals humanness or being; related ideas appear across Bantu languages, such as botho in Sotho.
It is also used commercially and politically, and critics warn of ubuntu branding and a gap between the ideal and everyday xenophobia in South Africa.
exampleEn: A community meeting decides to help a family rebuild after a fire, not as charity but as an obligation owed by neighbours who are part of the same personhood.
qualificationEn: Ubuntu is debated and often idealised, and it should not be flattened into a single doctrine covering all Bantu-speaking societies.

titleEn: The first shrine visit: how Japan starts the year
facts: Oshōgatsu, the New Year holiday, is Japan's most important annual festival; many businesses close for the first days of January and families gather around special meals.
Hatsumōde is the first shrine or temple visit of the year, usually made within the first three days of January; major shrines such as Meiji Jingū in Tokyo receive millions of visitors in that window.

Visitors draw omikuji fortune slips, buy omamori amulets and throw coins into the offering box; on New Year's Eve Buddhist temples ring the bell 108 times, the joya no kane, to remove the 108 earthly desires.
New Year food is symbolic: osechi ryōri in stacked lacquered boxes, ozōni soup with mochi, and black beans for health; children receive money in otoshidama envelopes from adults.
New Year cards, nengajō, are delivered on 1 January by a special postal arrangement, a system that email and messaging have reduced but not replaced.
exampleEn: On 2 January a family queues at a neighbourhood shrine, buys a fortune slip that says 'small luck', ties it to a pine branch and eats grilled mochi from a stall.
qualificationEn: Practice varies between Shinto, Buddhist, Christian and secular households, and some regions keep older lunar dates, so the three-day pattern is common rather than universal.

titleEn: Obon: the week the ancestors come home
facts: Obon is a Buddhist memorial season in mid-August in most of Japan, though some regions keep a mid-July date based on the lunar calendar.

Families believe ancestral spirits return home, so they clean graves, set small welcome fires called mukaebi and later send the spirits off with farewell fires; Kyoto's Gozan no Okuribi lights bonfires on five mountains on 16 August.
Bon odori dances are held in streets and parks around a wooden scaffold, with participants dancing regional folk steps in cotton yukata.
Many people travel back to ancestral hometowns, making Obon one of the country's heaviest domestic travel periods.
The season mixes Buddhist practice with family custom rather than a single doctrine, and some families without graves or temple ties mark it very little.
exampleEn: In a small town, the neighbourhood association sets up a yagura in the schoolyard, and families who moved to Tokyo come back for three days to dance and weed the family grave.
qualificationEn: Dates, dances and grave customs differ by region and Buddhist school, so Obon is not observed in the same way across Japan.

titleEn: The reunion dinner and the first sweep of the year
facts: Chinese New Year, the Spring Festival, begins on the second new moon after the winter solstice and ends with the Lantern Festival on the fifteenth day, so its date moves between late January and late February.
The reunion dinner on New Year's Eve is the emotional centre: fish is served and often deliberately left partly uneaten, since the word for fish sounds like surplus and abundance.
Red is everywhere, from couplets on doorframes to paper cuts and hongbao envelopes of money; a child may politely refuse a red envelope twice before accepting it.
Homes are cleaned before the festival to sweep away the old year, but sweeping on the first day is traditionally avoided so as not to sweep away good fortune.
The travel rush known as chunyun is the largest annual movement of people in the world, as migrants return to hometowns, and it shapes train and road congestion for weeks.
exampleEn: On New Year's Eve a family in Guangdong eats fish, dumplings and rice cakes, then leaves a coin under the plate and a light on before the first morning of the year.
qualificationEn: Foods, taboos and greetings differ sharply between north and south China and between rural and urban families, and many of the rules are folk beliefs rather than observances.

titleEn: Qingming: the spring ritual of tending graves
facts: Qingming, 'clear and bright', falls around 4 or 5 April and is one of the few Chinese festivals fixed by the solar calendar rather than the moon.
Families visit graves to sweep, weed, repaint inscriptions and leave offerings; paper money, paper houses and even paper phones are burned for the ancestors.
The day mixes ancestor veneration with spring outings: kite flying is traditional, and in the Jiangnan region people eat qingtuan, green glutinous rice balls coloured with mugwort.
Qingming became a public holiday in mainland China in 2008; it is now a major travel period and a focus of traffic and fire-safety warnings.
Online tomb-sweeping and virtual offerings have grown, and many cities restrict open burning of paper offerings for air quality reasons.
exampleEn: A family drives to a hillside cemetery, cuts the grass around a grandfather's stone, lays out oranges and a bottle of baijiu, and burns a bundle of paper money before heading home for lunch.
qualificationEn: Rites differ by region and religion, and burning restrictions vary by city, so not every family visits a grave in person.

titleEn: Chuseok: the harvest rite for the ancestors
facts: Chuseok falls on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, usually in September or early October, and is one of Korea's two biggest holidays, with three days off.
Families perform charye, an ancestral memorial rite, arranging food in a set order on a low table and bowing to the ancestors; they then visit graves to cut the grass, a task called beolcho.
Half-moon rice cakes called songpyeon are steamed with pine needles and shared; making them together is part of the holiday.
Jesa rites are also held at home on the anniversary of an ancestor's death, with food, wine and bows, and the format is often learned by daughters-in-law.
Chuseok is a huge travel period, and in Christian households the ancestral rite may be shortened, skipped or replaced with a family meal.
exampleEn: Before dawn on Chuseok, a family lays out fruit, fish and rice cakes in a fixed order, bows twice, then drives to the ancestral grave with a sickle for the grass.
qualificationEn: The food order and rites vary by region and family, and younger urban families increasingly travel or rest instead, which makes the preparation itself a source of generational friction.

titleEn: Holi: a day when the usual courtesies are suspended
facts: Holi falls on the full moon of the month of Phalguna, usually in March, and begins the night before with Holika Dahan, bonfires that mark the burning of the demoness Holika.
The next day people throw coloured powder, gulal, and water at neighbours and strangers, and the usual rules of dress and hierarchy are temporarily loosened.
The festival is especially associated with the Braj region around Mathura and Vrindavan, where Lathmar Holi in Barsana has women playfully beating men with sticks.
A common phrase, 'bura na mano, Holi hai' ('do not mind, it is Holi'), licenses behaviour that would otherwise be rude, and the day is also used to settle grudges.
Synthetic colours have caused skin and eye reactions, and some cities have promoted natural colours and water-saving versions.
exampleEn: In a Jaipur street, neighbours who have not spoken for months smear colour on each other's faces, laugh and share sweets, and the argument is treated as over.
qualificationEn: Holi is celebrated very differently by region, caste and community, and it is a much smaller event in parts of South India than the northern street version.

titleEn: How families investigate a match in India
facts: A majority of Indian marriages still involve family matchmaking, ranging from fully arranged to semi-arranged, where families introduce a possible partner and the couple decides.
A matrimonial profile, or bio-data, typically lists education, occupation, family background, caste or subcaste, income and sometimes a horoscope for kundali matching.
The first meeting often happens at home or in a public place with families present, and the couple may have only a few meetings before deciding.
Caste, religion, region and language remain strong filters, although online matrimonial sites and dating apps have widened the search and changed how introductions happen.
Dowry is illegal under the Dowry Prohibition Act of 1961, but the practice persists in various forms, and wedding costs and status displays are widely discussed social issues.
exampleEn: A family in Pune receives a proposal through a relative, checks the horoscope, meets the prospective bride's family over tea, and the two young people then talk on the phone for several weeks before agreeing.
qualificationEn: Arranged marriage is not one thing: urban professional matches, village alliances and cross-region marriages differ sharply, and coercion is a separate and contested issue.

sources.title: Arranged marriage in the Indian subcontinent

titleEn: Dashain: tika, jamara and the long walk home
facts: Dashain, also called Vijaya Dashami, is Nepal's longest Hindu festival, lasting about fifteen days in late September or October and celebrating the goddess Durga's victory over the buffalo demon Mahishasura.

On the tenth day, elders apply tika, a mixture of rice, yoghurt and vermilion, to younger relatives' foreheads and give jamara, barley sprouts grown in the dark, along with a gift of money called dakshina.
Kite flying and bamboo swings, ping, are part of the festival atmosphere, and animal sacrifice at some temples has been reduced or regulated under animal-welfare pressure.
It is the biggest family reunion of the year, with people travelling from Kathmandu and abroad to ancestral homes, and it is also a major shopping season.
The festival has state ceremonies as well as household ones, including the showing of the royal sword and, since the republic, official rituals at the presidential residence.
exampleEn: A migrant worker takes a crowded bus home, receives tika from his grandmother, ties barley sprouts behind his ear and eats goat curry with cousins he has not seen all year.
qualificationEn: Dashain is a Hindu festival not observed in the same way by all Nepalis, and practice differs by caste, region and religion.

titleEn: Pohela Boishakh: new year under the banyan tree
facts: Pohela Boishakh is the Bengali new year, celebrated on 14 April in Bangladesh; in West Bengal the traditional calendar can place it on 14 or 15 April.

In Dhaka the day opens with choral songs under the banyan tree at Ramna Batamul, and the Mangal Shobhajatra procession of giant masks and motifs was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2016.
Shops and traders keep the halkhata custom, closing old account books and inviting customers for sweets and a fresh ledger on the first day of the year.
Traditional food includes panta bhat, fermented rice soaked overnight, served with fried hilsa fish, and people dress in white and red.
The modern public form was shaped by the 1960s cultural movement in East Pakistan and became a symbol of secular Bengali identity after independence.
exampleEn: A Dhaka family rises early, walks to Ramna Park in white and red, watches the masks of Mangal Shobhajatra pass, then eats panta bhat with fried hilsa at a relative's house.
qualificationEn: Dhaka's programme is not the whole story: rural customs, halkhata practice and the West Bengal version all differ.

titleEn: A Pakistani wedding is a week of separate events
facts: A Pakistani wedding commonly spans several functions: mehndi, baraat, nikah, valima and sometimes rukhsati, and different families combine or separate them in different ways.
The nikah is the Islamic marriage contract; it requires the bride's consent, two witnesses and a mahr, the dower promised to the bride, and it is recorded in a nikah nama.
The mehndi is a henna night with songs and dancing, usually hosted by the bride's family, while the baraat is the groom's procession arriving for the ceremony.
The valima is a reception given by the groom's family, and the rukhsati is the formal departure of the bride with her new husband.
The scale of weddings is a public topic: families negotiate venues, guest lists and clothing, and the cost of display can create debt.
exampleEn: In Lahore, the bride's cousins sing around a dhol at the mehndi, the groom arrives the next evening with a flower-decorated car, and the nikah is signed in front of both families.
qualificationEn: Practice differs sharply between Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashtun and Baloch families, and between devout, secular and mixed households, so the big wedding is not universal.

titleEn: Shinbyu: a Burmese boy's season as a novice
facts: Shinbyu is a novitiation ceremony in which a boy, often between seven and fifteen, is temporarily ordained as a novice monk in Theravada Buddhism.
The ceremony is usually arranged in the school holidays or before the Buddhist Lent, and it is a merit-making act for the whole family.
The boy is dressed as a prince, in reference to Prince Siddhartha's renunciation, paraded in a procession on horseback or in a car, then has his head shaved and puts on robes.
The length of stay varies from a few days to a whole Lent period, and some men repeat the ordination later as adults.
Families with daughters sometimes hold an ear-boring ceremony, nahtwin, as a parallel coming-of-age rite rather than a novitiation.
exampleEn: A family in Mandalay hires a band, dresses their son in silk and gold, parades him through the ward, and the next morning he sits in the monastery courtyard with a shaved head and a bowl.
qualificationEn: Urban families may keep the ceremony short, and practice differs by region, income and monastic guidance.

titleEn: Songkran: water as blessing, water as play
facts: Songkran marks the Thai new year from 13 to 15 April, when water is poured over Buddha images and over elders' hands as a blessing for the coming year.
The original rite is rot nam dam hua, pouring scented water on elders' hands to ask forgiveness and receive blessings; the public street water fight is a later, larger phenomenon.
Families return home, clean houses and make merit at temples, sometimes bringing sand to build small pagodas in the temple grounds.
The festival has become a tourism draw with foam parties and concerts, and the holiday period is also notorious for road deaths, prompting annual safety campaigns.
Regional practice differs: Chiang Mai hosts a major street festival, while many southern and rural communities keep a quieter family and temple focus.
exampleEn: On the first morning, a Bangkok office worker pours scented water over her grandmother's hands, receives a blessing, and only later joins the water fight on Silom Road.
qualificationEn: The tourist image has overshadowed the domestic rite, and not everyone welcomes being splashed, so the blessing and the party should be described as related but distinct.

titleEn: Tết: the first visitor decides the year
facts: Tết Nguyên Đán is the Vietnamese lunar new year, falling between late January and mid-February, and it is the biggest holiday of the year, with weeks of travel and closed shops.
The first visitor to enter a home in the new year, the xông đất, is believed to shape the household's luck, so families may invite a suitable person deliberately and avoid unlucky guests.
On the twenty-third day of the twelfth lunar month, families send off the Kitchen God, Ông Táo, who is said to ride a carp to heaven to report on the household.
Homes are decorated with peach blossom in the north and apricot blossom in the south, and sticky-rice cakes, bánh chưng in the north and bánh tét in the south, are central foods.
Common taboos include not sweeping on the first days, avoiding breaking things and avoiding black or white clothing, though younger generations often treat them lightly.
exampleEn: A family in Hanoi cleans the house, releases a carp into the lake for the Kitchen God, and on the first morning welcomes a carefully chosen visitor who brings luck and a red envelope.
qualificationEn: Customs differ between north and south Vietnam and between Buddhist, Christian and secular households, and many taboos are observed socially rather than literally believed.

titleEn: Slametan: the Javanese meal that sets things right
facts: Slametan, also called selamatan, is a communal ritual meal in Java that marks births, circumcisions, marriages, house moves, harvests and deaths.
Neighbours are invited, food is served in banana leaves and the host gives a short speech in Javanese, followed by Arabic prayers and a shared meal.
The aim is to create slamet, a state of safety, well-being and social harmony, and to share merit with ancestors and the community.
Tumpeng, a cone of yellow rice surrounded by side dishes, is a common centrepiece, and distributing food afterwards is part of the obligation.

Some communities blend Islamic prayer with pre-Islamic Javanese practice, which reformist Muslims have criticised, and similar communal meals appear under other names, such as kenduri, across the archipelago.
exampleEn: A family moving into a new house invites the whole lane for a slametan, serves tumpeng and chicken, and the neighbours' attendance signals that the household now belongs.
qualificationEn: The ritual is Javanese-centred and should not be described as a single Indonesian custom; forms vary by region, religion and urban setting.

titleEn: Bayanihan: the promise that neighbours can move a house
facts: Bayanihan is a Filipino value of communal mutual aid, built on the word bayan, town or community; the national image is of men carrying a nipa hut on bamboo poles to a new site.
In rural practice it means shared labour at harvest, house-building and weddings, with the host providing food and the community providing hands.
The custom has been revived as a label for volunteer disaster response, overseas Filipino worker networks and neighbourhood drives after typhoons.
Anthropologists distinguish the older reciprocal labour system from the modern brand, and note that remittances and paid labour have replaced much of the physical sharing.
The image of carrying a whole house is largely symbolic today, but it remains the standard shorthand for Filipino solidarity.
exampleEn: After a typhoon, a barangay organises a bayanihan day: neighbours clear a fallen roof together, one family cooks for everyone, and the work finishes before noon.
qualificationEn: The hut-carrying image is a symbol rather than typical practice, and the reality varies between rural reciprocity, urban volunteering and state campaigns.

titleEn: Nowruz: seven things starting with sin
facts: Nowruz is the Persian new year at the spring equinox, on 20 or 21 March, and it is celebrated across Iran and neighbouring countries; UNESCO lists it as intangible heritage.
The haft-sin table holds seven items beginning with the letter sin: sabzeh (sprouts), samanu (wheat pudding), senjed (oleaster), seer (garlic), sib (apple), somaq (sumac) and serkeh (vinegar).
A mirror, painted eggs, a goldfish bowl and a copy of the Quran or Divan-e Hafez are often added, though the composition varies by family.
On the last Tuesday night before Nowruz, Chaharshanbe Suri is marked by jumping over bonfires and shouting 'give me your redness, take my yellowness'.
The thirteenth day, Sizdah Bedar, is spent outdoors, with families picnicking and throwing the sprouted greens into running water to send away bad luck.
exampleEn: A Tehran family sets the haft-sin on a table by the window, places a goldfish in a bowl, and on the thirteenth day drives to the foothills for a picnic by a stream.
qualificationEn: Haft-sin items, fire rituals and the table's religious additions differ by family and region, and Nowruz is not a single Iranian practice.

titleEn: The Georgian supra: a table with a conductor
facts: A supra is a Georgian feast combining food, wine and a formal sequence of toasts, presided over by the tamada, the toastmaster.
The tamada decides who speaks, in what order and when anyone drinks; a good one balances memory, humour and the mood of the room.
Toasts usually cover peace, homeland, parents, the deceased, friendship, love and the guests; a visitor may be invited to give one, and refusing is a social misstep.
The table fills with khinkali dumplings, khachapuri cheese bread, walnut and aubergine dishes, fresh herbs and wine, often homemade.
Supras mark weddings, birthdays and funerals; the funeral supra has a restrained tone and its own order of toasts.
exampleEn: At a birthday in Tbilisi, the tamada raises the first toast to peace, then to the hosts, then asks a guest to speak about her grandmother, and the table falls quiet.
qualificationEn: Styles differ between Kartli, Kakheti, the mountains and the diaspora, and heavy drinking is expected at some supras but not all.

titleEn: Hajj: five days that reshape a life
facts: Hajj is the annual pilgrimage to Mecca, obligatory once in a lifetime for Muslims who are able; it takes place in the twelfth Islamic month, with the main rites from the eighth to the thirteenth day.
Pilgrims enter ihram, a state of ritual purity marked by simple white clothing for men, then circle the Kaaba seven times, walk between Safa and Marwa and stand at Arafat on the ninth day.
The standing at Arafat is the central rite; after sunset pilgrims move to Muzdalifah, then stone the pillars at Mina and sacrifice an animal for Eid al-Adha.
Roughly two million pilgrims attend in most years, and each country receives a quota; Saudi authorities manage crowd flow, health and safety.
The experience is physically demanding, and most pilgrims describe exhaustion alongside spiritual intensity; many also visit Medina before or after.
exampleEn: A pilgrim from Indonesia wears the white ihram, joins the crowd on the plain of Arafat in the afternoon heat, and later shaves his head as the first sign that the pilgrimage is nearly complete.
qualificationEn: Rite details differ slightly between schools of law, and most Muslims never perform Hajj; the shorter Umrah is a different pilgrimage.

titleEn: Shabbat: the weekly stopping of the week
facts: Shabbat runs from sunset on Friday to nightfall on Saturday, beginning with candle-lighting and Kiddush over wine, and ending with Havdalah.
Observant Jews refrain from thirty-nine categories of work, including lighting fires, driving and handling money; the rules are interpreted by rabbinic authorities and differ between communities.
Friday dinner is the central family meal, with challah bread, songs and blessings; in many observant homes it is the main gathering of the week.
Shabbat also shapes public life in Israel: buses and trains largely stop, many shops close and streets in religious neighbourhoods become quiet.
Urban adaptations include eruv boundaries, Shabbat elevators and hotplates, which allow observant life inside modern buildings.
exampleEn: In Jerusalem, a family lights candles before sunset, eats dinner with grandparents, and walks to synagogue in the morning while the main road stays empty.
qualificationEn: Observance ranges from strictly Orthodox to secular, and the public character of Shabbat varies sharply between cities and neighbourhoods.

titleEn: Hıdırellez: wishes tied to trees in early May
facts: Hıdırellez falls on the night of 5 to 6 May and marks the meeting of the prophets Hızır and İlyas, understood as the arrival of spring and the beginning of the fertile season.
People jump over fires, make wishes and tie small cloths or paper wishes to trees, especially a wish tree, and some throw written wishes into running water.
The day is traditionally spent outdoors with picnics, music and special foods, and young people use it for omens about marriage and future partners.
The date belongs to the old Rumi calendar and is also called Ruz-ı Hızır; it is a cultural and folk celebration rather than an official public holiday.
UNESCO inscribed the spring celebration Hıdırellez, jointly with North Macedonia, on its intangible heritage list in 2017.
exampleEn: On the evening of 5 May, a family in Izmir lights a small fire in the garden, jumps over it, ties a ribbon to a fig tree with a wish and shares a picnic the next day.
qualificationEn: Rituals vary widely between Turkish regions, Balkan communities and urban celebrations, and many people treat it simply as a spring festival.

titleEn: Sobremesa: the hour after the plates are cleared
facts: Sobremesa literally means 'over the table': the time after the food is finished when people stay seated and keep talking, often over coffee or a digestif.
It is distinct from dessert; the point is the conversation, and clearing the table immediately is read as hurrying guests out.
It is strongest at long weekend lunches with family and friends, and restaurant staff generally do not bring the bill until asked.
The practice reflects a Mediterranean social pattern of long mid-day meals and late dinners rather than a schedule built around efficiency.
Sobremesa is under pressure from longer working hours and commuting, but it remains a recognised marker of Spanish social life, with the word used in advertising and tourism.
exampleEn: After a Sunday paella in Valencia, the plates are cleared but nobody moves; coffee, a bottle of orujo and a conversation about a cousin's new job stretch for another ninety minutes.
qualificationEn: Sobremesa is an ideal as much as a routine: weekday lunches are short, and not every family lingers or wants to.

titleEn: The Palio: a horse race that organises a city
facts: The Palio di Siena is a bareback horse race run twice a year, on 2 July and 16 August, in the sloping shell-shaped Piazza del Campo.
Ten of Siena's seventeen contrade, the neighbourhood associations with their own colours, churches and rivalries, compete in each race.
The race lasts well under two minutes, and a horse that finishes riderless can still win for its contrada, which receives the painted palio banner.
Before the race, the contradaioli parade in Renaissance costume in the corteo storico, and the horse is blessed in its contrada church.
The Palio structures the year: contrada membership is usually inherited through family and neighbourhood, and alliances and rivalries shape local social life.
exampleEn: On 16 August, a Sienese family walks to its contrada's church for the horse blessing, then crowds onto the piazza while their jockey rides a risky line along the outer wall.
qualificationEn: The Palio is deeply local to Siena and its seventeen contrade, not a general Italian custom, and access to the inner square is controlled.

titleEn: The galette, the bean and the youngest child under the table
facts: On Epiphany, 6 January, and through much of January, French bakeries sell the galette des Rois, a puff-pastry cake filled with frangipane, or in the south a ring-shaped brioche with candied fruit.
A fève, originally a dried bean and now usually a small ceramic figurine, is hidden in the cake; whoever finds it becomes king or queen and wears a paper crown.
The cake is cut into equal slices, and a youngest child often sits under the table calling out who receives each slice, a device meant to guarantee fairness.
In some families a slice is set aside as la part du pauvre, the poor man's share, recalling older customs of hospitality; in others the fève collection becomes a family hobby.
The custom has religious roots in the Magi but is largely secular today, and the season is one of the bakery trade's busiest.
exampleEn: At a family lunch in Lyon, the youngest cousin sits under the table and shouts names and the hidden porcelain figure turns up in the grandmother's slice, making her queen for the afternoon.
qualificationEn: The northern frangipane galette and the southern brioche are different pastries, and the rituals around cutting and hiding the fève vary by family and region.

titleEn: Oktoberfest is a Munich wedding anniversary
facts: Oktoberfest began in 1810 with the wedding of Crown Prince Ludwig, later King Ludwig I, to Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen; a horse race on 17 October was repeated the following year.
It is held on the Theresienwiese, the meadow named after the bride, and lasts about sixteen to eighteen days, ending on the first Sunday of October unless 3 October extends it.
Only breweries inside Munich's city limits may supply the main tents, and beer is served by the litre in heavy glass Mass mugs.
The festival has fourteen large tents and many smaller ones; reservations are needed months ahead, and visitors often wear lederhosen or dirndl.
The Oide Wiesn, a heritage section with old rides and a museum tent, was added in 2010 and is now a regular feature of the festival.
exampleEn: A Munich office books a table in a tent for a colleague's birthday, and the group arrives at 9 a.m. to secure seats, order a Mass and a roast chicken, and listen to a brass band.
qualificationEn: Oktoberfest is a Munich festival, not a national German custom: many Germans have never attended, and Bavarian traditions differ from those of other regions.

titleEn: Krampus: the frightening half of December
facts: Krampus is a horned, fur-covered figure in Alpine folklore who accompanies Saint Nicholas on the evening of 5 December, Krampusnacht, in Austria, Bavaria, Switzerland and neighbouring regions.
While Nicholas rewards good children, Krampus carries chains and birch branches and traditionally threatens to carry bad children away in a sack.
Young men wear hand-carved wooden masks and animal skins for Krampuslauf processions, and masks are often carved locally and passed down.
The figure has pre-Christian roots, possibly linked to Perchten and winter spirit processions, but its pairing with Saint Nicholas is documented from the Middle Ages.
In parts of the twentieth century Krampus was suppressed by church and state authorities, and today the processions are both a local identity marker and a tourist attraction.
exampleEn: In a Salzburg village on 5 December, masked Krampus figures rattle chains through the street while children hide behind their parents, and Saint Nicholas hands out nuts and oranges.
qualificationEn: Krampus is regional, not a general Austrian Christmas custom, and many families keep the figure mild or avoid it for small children.

titleEn: The Röstigraben: Switzerland's border in the head
facts: Röstigraben, 'rösti ditch', is the informal name for the cultural and political divide between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland, named after the potato dish.
The term became common in the twentieth century and is often illustrated by referendum results in which the French-speaking west voted differently from the German-speaking centre and east.
The 1992 referendum on joining the European Economic Area is the classic example: French-speaking cantons voted yes, German-speaking ones no, and the proposal failed narrowly.
There is no line on the ground: the divide is statistical and cultural, softened by commuting, bilingualism and shared federal institutions, and Italian-speaking Ticino forms another axis.
Rösti itself is a grated potato cake associated with German-speaking Switzerland, though it is eaten across the country, so the dish is a symbol rather than a real boundary marker.
exampleEn: A news programme shows a map after a Sunday vote: the west is one colour and the centre-east another, and commentators immediately name the Röstigraben.
qualificationEn: The Röstigraben is an analytical metaphor, not a description of every person, and it has narrowed on many issues.

titleEn: Sinterklaas and the changing face of Zwarte Piet
facts: Sinterklaas is celebrated on 5 December, pakjesavond, after a bishop-like figure arrives from Spain by steamboat in mid-November and rides through towns with his helpers.
Children put their shoes out with a carrot for the horse and receive small gifts; the main presents are often wrapped as surprises with accompanying joke poems signed by Sinterklaas.
Zwarte Piet, the helper, was historically performed with blackface, curly wigs and red lips, a depiction that has become the centre of a public conflict.
Since the 2010s many schools, broadcasters and municipalities have switched to Roetveegpiet, a soot-smudge version, and the 2019 national entry broadcast used only that form.
The debate is a live case of a tradition changing under social pressure, with defenders of the old figure and opponents, including many Black Dutch citizens, disagreeing about history and racism.
exampleEn: At a primary school in Utrecht, children sing welcome songs as a soot-faced Piet hands out pepernoten, while parents in the playground discuss the school's choice of costume.
qualificationEn: Practice now varies by city, school and broadcaster, and Dutch people hold widely different views, so the topic should not be reduced to a single national position.

titleEn: The Sunday roast: a meal that kept the week in order
facts: The Sunday roast is a British meal of roast meat with potatoes, vegetables, gravy and often Yorkshire pudding, traditionally eaten at mid-day on Sunday.
Its roots are in medieval Sunday feasting and the industrial workweek, when Sunday was the one day off; meat was put in the oven before church and finished after the service.
Regional pairings matter: Yorkshire pudding with beef, sage and onion stuffing with pork, mint sauce with lamb, and horseradish with beef.
The pub carvery and the Sunday lunch menu keep the tradition commercial, and many families still gather for it even as weekly church attendance has declined.
The meal carries strong nostalgia in British culture, and in cities Caribbean and South Asian Sunday lunches have reshaped what the meal looks like.
exampleEn: On a rainy Sunday in Sheffield, three generations sit down at one o'clock to beef, Yorkshire puddings and gravy, and the washing-up is left until the afternoon film.
qualificationEn: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have distinct food traditions, and the Sunday roast is not universal: many British households never cook it.

titleEn: The Eisteddfod: a language kept by competition
facts: An eisteddfod is a Welsh festival of literature, music and performance, and the National Eisteddfod, held in August and moving between north and south Wales, is conducted largely in Welsh.
Its centrepiece is the chairing of the bard, when the winner of the strict-metre poetry competition, the awdl, is honoured by the Gorsedd of Bards in white, blue and green robes.
Competitions cover recitation, solo and choral singing, instrumental music and folk dance, and the surrounding field, the Maes, holds stalls, food and the pavilion.
The National Eisteddfod dates from 1861 and grew out of earlier eisteddfodau; it is a key institution of the Welsh language and a social reunion for Welsh speakers.
There are also local eisteddfodau and the Urdd youth eisteddfod, and the Gorsedd's druidic ceremonial has long attracted both affection and criticism.
exampleEn: In a packed pavilion, the Archdruid calls for peace, a trumpet sounds, and the winning poet is escorted to the chair while the audience stands.
qualificationEn: The National Eisteddfod is a Welsh-language event with its own rules, and non-Welsh speakers, as well as many Welsh people, experience it differently.

titleEn: The Irish wake: three days of tea and stories
facts: An Irish wake traditionally takes place in the family home in the days between death and burial, with the deceased laid out in a room and neighbours calling to pay respects.
Hospitality is central: tea, sandwiches, cake and often alcohol are served, and visitors share stories about the deceased, with laughter alongside grief.
Older customs included stopping clocks, covering mirrors and lighting candles, and keening, the caoineadh, was performed by women as a formal lament.
Keening largely died out in the twentieth century, and city wakes have increasingly moved to funeral homes, but the visitation and the tea remain.
The wake is followed by removal to the church, a funeral Mass in Catholic practice, and burial, and it is often described as a social event as much as a religious one.
exampleEn: In a kitchen in rural Mayo, neighbours arrive with sandwich platters, sit with the family until midnight, and tell a story about the deceased's prize-winning sheep.
qualificationEn: Practice varies by religion, region and family, and the 'wild Irish wake' stereotype exaggerates the drinking and misrepresents a usually sober occasion.

titleEn: Fika: the coffee break you are expected to take
facts: Fika is the Swedish institution of a coffee break, usually with something sweet such as a kanelbulle, the cinnamon bun, and often taken at set times in workplaces.
It is a verb as well as a noun, att fika, and it implies sitting down to talk rather than drinking coffee on the move.
The word is twentieth-century slang, often explained as a playful reversal of kaffe, coffee, and it became general in the early 1900s.
Many workplaces have a collective fika twice a day, and bringing cake or buns to the office for a birthday is a common obligation.
Fika carries an egalitarian ethos: managers and staff sit together, and the break is a place where hierarchy is supposed to soften.
exampleEn: At 3 p.m. the office kitchen fills for fika, someone cuts a princess cake, and the meeting that ran late is postponed until after the coffee.
qualificationEn: Not every Swede fikas daily, and the commercial 'fika lifestyle' image oversimplifies a practice that varies by workplace and region.

titleEn: Sauna: Finland's everyday room
facts: Finland has around three million saunas for a population of about 5.5 million, so the sauna is a household or building fixture rather than a luxury.
The classic Finnish sauna is heated by wood, with the smoke sauna, savusauna, as the oldest form; temperatures are usually between 80 and 100 degrees Celsius.
The rhythm alternates heat with cooling: stepping outside, rolling in snow, swimming in a lake or taking a cold shower between rounds.
Saunas have been used for washing, healing and major life events; historically babies were born in them and the dead were prepared there.
Finnish sauna culture was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2020, and etiquette includes a towel, quiet talk and respecting others' space.
exampleEn: On a summer evening at a lakeside cottage, a family heats the wood sauna, sits inside with birch whisk bundles, then runs down the jetty to jump into the lake.
qualificationEn: Public saunas and home saunas follow different rules, and sauna culture varies between Finland, Sweden, Russia and the Baltic states.

titleEn: Hygge: the ordinary practice of shelter
facts: Hygge, roughly cosiness or comfortable togetherness, describes a mood of shelter, warmth and ease: candles, blankets, warm drinks and unhurried time with others.
The word is related to an old Norwegian term for shelter and well-being, and it entered Danish in the nineteenth century, becoming a cultural keyword in the twentieth.
It is ordinary rather than luxurious: a candle on the table, a simple meal with friends, a sofa and a blanket; the commercial design version is a later export.
Danes often invoke hygge in winter, when daylight is short, and it is used as a noun, a verb and an adjective, hyggeligt.
Anthropologists note that hygge also marks inclusion and exclusion: the warm circle can be a way of defining who belongs at the table.
exampleEn: On a dark November evening, a Copenhagen family lights candles, makes a pot of coffee and sits under blankets with a board game instead of going out.
qualificationEn: Hygge is Danish, with Norwegian koselig as a close but not identical relative, and the wellness-industry version is not how Danes usually use the word.

titleEn: Bunad: wearing a region on 17 May
facts: A bunad is a Norwegian traditional costume, distinguished by embroidery, silver jewellery and woven wool, and designs are tied to specific regions and valleys.
Most bunads were reconstructed in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries from older folk dress and national-romantic research, so they are not unchanged medieval clothing.
A complete bunad is expensive, often costing tens of thousands of kroner, and can take years to assemble; many are inherited or made to order.
On 17 May, Constitution Day, streets fill with bunads alongside suits and school marching bands, and the greeting is 'Gratulerer med dagen', congratulations on the day.
Local bunad councils approve designs and advise on correct use, and the silver jewellery, sølje, is often a family heirloom.
exampleEn: On 17 May in Bergen, a grandmother fastens her granddaughter's silver brooch, adjusts the apron and joins the school parade in the rain.
qualificationEn: Many Norwegians do not own a bunad, and the Sámi gákti is a distinct national dress that should not be confused with it.

titleEn: Wigilia: the empty chair at Poland's Christmas Eve
facts: Wigilia is the Polish Christmas Eve supper, which begins when the first star appears and opens with the sharing of opłatek, a thin Christmas wafer, and mutual wishes.
The meal is traditionally meatless and often has twelve dishes, including carp, herring, mushroom soup, pierogi, sauerkraut and dried-fruit compote.
An extra place is set for an unexpected guest or an absent family member, and hay is sometimes placed under the tablecloth in memory of the manger.
Gifts are opened after supper, and Christmas Day is the church feast; 25 and 26 December are public holidays in Poland.
The custom is documented in Polish gentry culture from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and was strengthened by national-romantic movements, with strong regional variants.
exampleEn: At dusk on 24 December, a family in Kraków shares opłatek and wishes, eats twelve meatless dishes, leaves one chair empty and then opens presents under the tree.
qualificationEn: The number of dishes and the exact menu vary by family and region, and many households now simplify the meal.

titleEn: Malanka: masked carols in the old New Year
facts: Malanka falls on the night of 13 to 14 January in the Julian calendar and is the Ukrainian folk new year, named after Saint Melania.
Groups of masked villagers go from house to house with carols called shchedrivky and short comic plays; the Goat, Koza, and a character called Malanka are central figures.
Costumes of bear, gypsy, doctor and grandparents vary by region, and in some villages Malanka is played by a man dressed as a woman.
The ritual was discouraged during the Soviet period and revived after 1991, especially in western Ukraine, where village groups compete in performances.
It overlaps with Shchedry Vechir, the generous evening of 13 January, when families hold a festive dinner before the carolling.
exampleEn: In a Carpathian village, a masked group bangs on a door, performs a short comic scene with the Goat, and collects sweets as the household laughs and invites them in.
qualificationEn: Malanka's dates and forms are contested after Ukraine's recent calendar reform, and regional and diaspora versions differ considerably.

titleEn: Maslenitsa: butter, blini and the burning of winter
facts: Maslenitsa is the East Slavic festival of the week before Great Lent, marked by blini, sledding, bonfires and the burning of a straw effigy of Lady Maslenitsa.
Each day of the week has a name and a role, from the Monday meeting to Wide Thursday and Forgiveness Sunday, when people ask forgiveness of relatives and friends.
The round blini and the bonfire carry pre-Christian sun and spring symbolism, partly absorbed into the Orthodox calendar; the Soviet state reframed it as a secular seeing-off of winter.
Dairy foods are allowed but meat is already excluded before Lent, so blini are eaten with butter, sour cream, caviar, jam or fish.
In cities the week is marked by fairs and concerts, while in villages sledding, snow-fort games and family visits persist.
exampleEn: On Forgiveness Sunday a family eats blini with sour cream, asks each other's forgiveness, and in the evening a straw effigy burns in a field outside the village.
qualificationEn: Maslenitsa practice differs across Russia, Belarus and Ukraine, and many urban Russians treat it as a fair rather than a religious observance.

titleEn: The altar at the end of October: Día de Muertos
facts: Día de Muertos is celebrated on 1 and 2 November, with regional extensions, when families believe the dead return to visit the living.
Ofrendas, altars built in homes and sometimes in cemeteries, hold photographs, favourite foods and drinks, marigolds, candles, papel picado and sugar skulls.
In some communities families clean and decorate graves and spend the night at the cemetery; Michoacán, Oaxaca and Mexico City each have distinct traditions.
The festival mixes Mesoamerican ancestor practices with Catholic All Saints' and All Souls' days, and UNESCO inscribed it on its intangible heritage list in 2008.
La Catrina, the elegant skeleton, comes from the satirical prints of José Guadalupe Posada in the early twentieth century, not from pre-Hispanic dress.
exampleEn: A family in Oaxaca builds an ofrenda with a grandmother's photograph, a plate of mole, marigolds and a glass of mezcal, and the scent of copal fills the room.
qualificationEn: Día de Muertos is not Mexican Halloween: it is regionally varied, partly religious, and in some towns quieter and more domestic than the street version.

titleEn: Quinceañera: fifteen, a Mass and a first dance
facts: A quinceañera marks a girl's fifteenth birthday, usually with a Catholic thanksgiving Mass and a party, and is a coming-of-age celebration across Mexico and Latin America.
The celebration includes a court of honour of friends and chambelanes, a waltz, a change from flat shoes to heels and a first dance with the father.
The Mass and blessing are often central, though the party may be largely secular; some families choose a trip or a smaller meal instead of a large event.
The tradition blends Spanish colonial, Indigenous and Catholic elements, and in Mexican-American communities it often mixes with the American Sweet 16.
The dress, the brindis toast and the last doll, the última muñeca, are familiar features, though local and family variants are strong.
exampleEn: In a Monterrey parish hall, the birthday girl arrives in a wide dress, the priest blesses her, and after Mass she changes shoes and dances a waltz with her father and the court.
qualificationEn: Not every Mexican girl has a quinceañera, costs can be high, and many families celebrate more simply or not at all.

titleEn: Potlatch: the feast where wealth is given away
facts: Potlatch is a ceremonial feast and gift-giving practice among Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest, including the Kwakwakaʼwakw, Tlingit, Haida and Nuu-chah-nulth.
Hosts distribute food and goods to guests and display inherited rights to names, songs, masks and histories, so the event validates status and honours the dead.
The Canadian government banned potlatch in 1885, and prosecutions such as the 1921 arrest of Chief Dan Cranmer's guests led to confiscation of regalia; the ban was lifted in 1951.
The ceremony survived underground and remains a living practice; museums and governments have repatriated regalia in recent decades.
Early anthropologists read it as conspicuous consumption, but it is better understood as a legal and social institution regulating titles, marriage and reciprocity.
exampleEn: At a coastal village gathering, a family hosts hundreds of guests, gives away blankets and food, and announces a inherited name for a granddaughter in front of witnesses.
qualificationEn: There are many distinct Nations with different protocols, and some ceremonies are restricted; potlatch is not a historical re-enactment or a public show.

titleEn: Rumspringa: the Amish years before baptism
facts: Rumspringa, Pennsylvania Dutch for 'running around', is the period in some Amish communities when adolescents around sixteen are not yet baptised and may socialise more freely.
It is not a universal Amish institution: its length and content vary by affiliation, settlement and family, and some communities have little of it.
Young people may attend singings, use a limited phone or own a buggy, and date; baptism usually follows in the late teens or early twenties.
Baptism means accepting the Ordnung, the church's rules; those who leave after baptism may face shunning, Meidung.
The popular image of wild rebellion, spread by the 2002 documentary Devil's Playground, is exaggerated: most Amish youth eventually join the church.
exampleEn: A Lancaster County teenager spends Sunday evenings at a singing in a barn, borrows a cousin's phone, and is baptised two years later in front of the congregation.
qualificationEn: The Amish are not one group, and practice differs between Old Order, New Order and Swartzentruber communities; Lancaster County is not representative of all.

titleEn: Kwanzaa: seven days of names and principles
facts: Kwanzaa was created in 1966 by Maulana Karenga, a professor of Africana studies, and first celebrated in Los Angeles; it runs from 26 December to 1 January.
It is built on seven principles, the Nguzo Saba: unity, self-determination, collective work, cooperative economics, purpose, creativity and faith.
A kinara holds seven candles, one for each principle, and a mkeka mat, crops, corn and a unity cup are displayed; the greeting 'Habari gani?' is answered with the day's principle.
Gifts are often handmade or educational, and the celebration draws on Swahili terms and pan-African motifs as well as harvest imagery.
It is a cultural rather than religious holiday, observed by a minority of African Americans, and its modern invention and its founder's politics have both been criticised.
exampleEn: On the second night, a family lights two candles on the kinara, a child answers 'kujichagulia' to the greeting, and everyone shares a small handmade gift.
qualificationEn: Kwanzaa is not an African or a Christian holiday, and most African Americans do not observe it; family practice varies widely.

titleEn: Juneteenth: the date freedom was announced in Texas
facts: Juneteenth, on 19 June, marks the day in 1865 when Major General Gordon Granger announced General Order No. 3 in Galveston, declaring the freedom of enslaved people in Texas.
The news came more than two years after the Emancipation Proclamation, which had applied to states in rebellion, and Texas enslavers had withheld it.
Early celebrations were called Jubilee Day and included prayer, readings of the Emancipation Proclamation, singing and food, with red drinks and red velvet cake as traditional dishes.
Texas made Juneteenth an official state holiday in 1980, other states followed, and it became a federal holiday in 2021.
Galveston and Houston remain centres of commemoration, and many families use the date for reunions and community picnics.
exampleEn: In Galveston, a family attends a morning reading of the 1865 order at the historical marker, then joins a park picnic with red soda and barbecue.
qualificationEn: Juneteenth marks a specific Texas announcement, not the single end of slavery nationwide, and commemorations differ widely among communities.

titleEn: At the sugar shack: Quebec's spring ritual
facts: A cabane à sucre, sugar shack, is a maple-syrup producer's establishment where sap is boiled down and visitors eat a traditional meal during the spring sugaring season.
The season runs roughly from March to April, when daytime thaw and cold nights make maple sap run; the meal typically includes ham, baked beans, omelette and oreilles de crisse, pork rinds.
Maple taffy, tire sur la neige, is poured onto snow and rolled onto a stick, and children are taken to sugar shacks on school trips.
Quebec produces the majority of the world's maple syrup, and the industry is regulated by a producer federation with quotas.
Maple sap harvesting was practised by Indigenous peoples before European settlement, and the sugar shack as a public meal is a later French-Canadian institution.
exampleEn: In April, a family drives to a shack outside Trois-Rivières, eats pea soup and ham at long communal tables, then rolls warm syrup on snow in the yard.
qualificationEn: Sugar shacks are a Quebec and Appalachian tradition rather than a national Canadian one, and commercial shacks range from working farms to large banquet halls.

titleEn: Vodou: serving the lwa in Haiti
facts: Haitian Vodou is a religion that developed among enslaved Africans and their descendants, blending West African traditions, especially Fon, Yoruba and Kongo, with Catholic elements.
It centres on a distant creator, Bondye, and on spirits called lwa, served through drumming, dancing, singing, offerings and possession, when a lwa 'mounts' a participant.
A manbo, priestess, or oungan, priest, leads a community; ceremonies follow ritual calendars, and Catholic saints are often associated with particular lwa.
Colonial authorities banned African religious practice under the 1685 Code Noir, and the religion was later misrepresented in films and travel writing.
Vodou is a living religion in Haiti and its diaspora; the 'voodoo doll' is a commercial invention, not a Haitian Vodou practice.
exampleEn: At a peristyle in Port-au-Prince, drummers build a rhythm, a woman in white begins to shake, and the community recognises the lwa who has arrived and greets it with songs and offerings.
qualificationEn: Rituals vary between houses and regions and some are restricted, so Vodou should not be described as a single system or reduced to the Hollywood stereotype.

titleEn: Festa Junina: bonfires and square dances in June
facts: Festa Junina is a June festival honouring Saint Anthony on 13 June, Saint John on 24 June and Saint Peter on 29 June, brought to Brazil by Portuguese colonisers.
It mixes Catholic devotion with rural food and music: quadrilha square dancing, forró, bonfires and decorations of paper flags and straw hats.
Participants dress as caipiras, country people, with checked shirts, straw hats and painted freckles, and the festival is a school and neighbourhood event as much as a religious one.
Corn is the seasonal centrepiece: pamonha, curau, canjica, milho and paçoca, with quentão, a ginger and cachaça drink, and mulled wine.
The Northeast holds the largest celebrations, especially Campina Grande and Caruaru, while the Amazon has the Boi-Bumbá festivals of Parintins in the same season.
exampleEn: At a school in Recife, children in straw hats dance quadrilha around a bonfire made of coloured paper, and parents buy corn cakes and quentão from stalls.
qualificationEn: Celebrations range from small school parties to huge festivals, and the caipira costume carries rural stereotypes that are sometimes contested.

region: Río de la Plata and Paraguay
titleEn: Mate: the gourd that goes round the circle
facts: Yerba mate is an infusion drunk from a gourd, the mate, through a metal straw, the bombilla, and it is usually shared in a circle in Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and southern Brazil.
The host, the cebador, pours hot water, drinks the first gourd to test it, then refills and passes the mate in turn; each person finishes the gourd before it returns.
Saying 'gracias' means 'no more, thank you'; accepting and passing the gourd back without a word means you want another round.
Etiquette warns against stirring the bombilla, rushing the cebador or adding sugar without asking, and carrying a thermos and mate set is ordinary.
The drink comes from the Guaraní and was spread by Jesuit missions and gaucho culture; in Paraguay it is often drunk cold as tereré.
exampleEn: On a Buenos Aires bus queue, a man fills his gourd from a thermos under his arm, offers it to a friend, and the friend says gracias after one round to signal he is done.
qualificationEn: Rules differ across the four countries and between families, and mate is deeply sociable but also frequently drunk alone.

titleEn: Inti Raymi: Cusco re-stages the sun festival
facts: Inti Raymi is the Inca festival of the sun, held near the June solstice; the modern version is a theatrical re-enactment staged in Cusco on 24 June.
The performance begins at Qorikancha, the former Sun Temple, and moves to the fortress of Sacsayhuamán, with actors playing the Sapa Inca, priests and nobles, largely in Quechua.
The modern staging dates from 1944, when Cusco intellectuals led by Humberto Vidal Unda revived the ceremony as a civic spectacle.
The historical Inca festival honoured Inti with sacrifices and processions, and colonial authorities suppressed it in the 1570s under Viceroy Francisco de Toledo.
Today it is a major tourist event and a source of local identity, with schools, dance groups and neighbourhood organisations taking part in the preceding weeks.
exampleEn: On 24 June, crowds line the road from Qorikancha to Sacsayhuamán as a procession in woven costumes carries the Sapa Inca on a litter, with conch shells sounding.
qualificationEn: The modern Inti Raymi is a twentieth-century theatrical revival, not an unbroken Inca rite, and it is one Andean festival among many.

titleEn: Alasitas: buying next year in miniature
facts: Alasitas is a January festival in La Paz and other Bolivian cities centred on Ekeko, the smiling Andean figure of abundance, and on miniature goods.
Participants buy tiny models of what they hope to gain in the coming year: houses, cars, money, university degrees and passports, and have them blessed.
The fair is a huge market where artisans sell miniatures, miniature banknotes and property deeds; many people buy objects they cannot yet afford in full size.
The tradition has pre-Hispanic Andean roots and was later linked to the feast of Our Lady of La Paz, so it mixes Catholic and Indigenous elements.
The Ekeko is traditionally given as a gift and is believed to bring prosperity if treated well, and the festival is one of the city's biggest commercial events.
exampleEn: A student buys a miniature diploma and a tiny house at the January fair, takes them to a yatiri for a blessing with incense, and keeps them on a shelf at home.
qualificationEn: Alasitas is strongest in La Paz, and related miniature fairs in other Andean cities have different dates and forms.

titleEn: Barranquilla: four days of carnival on the Caribbean coast
facts: The Carnival of Barranquilla is held in the four days before Ash Wednesday, usually in February or March, and is Colombia's largest carnival.
It opens with the Batalla de Flores, the Battle of Flowers parade, and includes the Gran Parada and the Guacherna night parade.
The marimonda, a masked jester figure, is the emblem of the carnival, alongside cumbia, mapalé and chandé dances and music.
UNESCO declared it a Masterpiece of Oral and Intangible Heritage in 2003, and the city's Caribbean port identity shapes the mix of European, African and Indigenous elements.
Neighbourhood groups, grupos de barrio, plan and compete all year, and the character Joselito Carnaval 'dies' at the end of the festivities.
exampleEn: On the Saturday before Ash Wednesday, a family stakes out a curb on Via 40 to watch the Batalla de Flores, while marimonda figures in long-nosed masks dance past the floats.
qualificationEn: The dates move with Ash Wednesday, and the carnival is specific to Barranquilla and the Caribbean coast rather than a national Colombian custom.

titleEn: Fiestas Patrias: the eighteenth of September
facts: Chile's Fiestas Patrias are held on 18 and 19 September, marking the 1810 junta that began the independence process and, on the second day, Army Day.
The celebrations centre on fondas and ramadas, temporary halls and stalls with food, music and dancing, where cueca, the national dance, is performed.
Typical foods include empanadas, anticuchos and chicha or terremoto, a sweet wine cocktail; kite flying, volantines, is a seasonal custom.
The declaration of independence was signed in February 1818, but the September dates commemorate the first governing junta, which is why the holiday is called the eighteenth.
Military parades take place in Santiago and other cities on 19 September, and the week is a major travel and family period.
exampleEn: On the afternoon of the 18th, a Santiago family drives to a fonda in a park, eats empanadas, dances one cueca and lets the children fly a kite.
qualificationEn: Customs differ from the Aymara north to the Mapuche south, and some Chileans criticise the holiday's drinking culture and nationalist display.

titleEn: Candombe: the drums that belong to a neighbourhood
facts: Candombe is an Afro-Uruguayan music and dance tradition with roots among enslaved Africans brought to Montevideo and the Río de la Plata.
It is performed by comparsas with three drums, chico, repique and piano, plus a madera rhythm section, and dancers in colourful costumes.
The annual Llamadas festival in February fills the streets of the Barrio Sur and Palermo neighbourhoods with drumming, and those areas remain the tradition's heart.
UNESCO inscribed Uruguayan candombe on its Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2009.
The tradition is tied to Afro-Uruguayan community life and has been incorporated into national identity, prompting debates about appropriation and commercialisation.
exampleEn: During the Llamadas, a comparsa from Barrio Sur turns a corner with forty drummers in formation, the low chico drums keeping time while the repique improvises.
qualificationEn: Candombe also names different Afro-diasporic traditions in Argentina and Brazil, so the Uruguayan form should be specified.

community: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
titleEn: Welcome to Country: what the words actually do
facts: A Welcome to Country is a formal protocol delivered by Traditional Owners at the start of a significant event on their Country, and may include speech, song, smoke or dance.
It is distinct from an Acknowledgement of Country, which anyone present can offer, naming the Traditional Owners and their continuing custodianship.
The protocol spread through Australian public institutions from the 1990s and 2000s, and the opening of parliament now commonly includes one.
Authority matters: a Welcome must come from the right people for that Country, not from any Aboriginal person, and using it without authority can cause offence.
In Indigenous English, Country means the ancestral land with which a person has a relationship of obligation, not a national territory.
exampleEn: At a university graduation, an Elder from the local nation welcomes the audience in language and English before the ceremony begins.
qualificationEn: Protocols vary enormously between language groups, and not every event includes one; visitors may give an Acknowledgement, never a Welcome.

titleEn: Tangihanga: three days on the marae
facts: Tangihanga is the Māori funeral rite, usually lasting several days on a marae, with the deceased lying in an open casket in the wharenui, the meeting house, while visitors pay respects.
The body is greeted with speeches, whaikōrero, songs, waiata, and karanga, the ceremonial calls usually given by women.
Mourners often stay overnight and share food; burial usually occurs on the third day, followed by a hākari feast and later a hura kōhatu, the unveiling of the headstone.
Tikanga, protocol, governs seating, speaking order and the roles of manuhiri, visitors, and tangata whenua, hosts.
The ritual continues in urban and diaspora life, with marae-based tangihanga and adaptations, and many Pākehā encounter it through work or community.
exampleEn: At a marae outside Rotorua, visitors are called onto the courtyard, remove their shoes, greet the deceased with a speech and song, then share a meal in the dining hall.
qualificationEn: Marae protocols differ between iwi and hapū, and not all Māori whānau follow the same format, so visitors should ask rather than assume.

titleEn: Fa'a Samoa: the values behind the welcome
facts: Fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way, names a way of life built on fa'aaloalo, respect, alofa, love and compassion, and feagaiga, the sacred covenant between brother and sister.
The matai chiefly system organises village life: matai titles are conferred by family councils, and village fono councils regulate land, behaviour and ceremonies.
The extended family, aiga, pools resources and remittances from relatives overseas, and church life and Sunday observance are central in most villages.
Formal welcomes include the 'ava, kava, ceremony and the exchange of fine mats, ie toga, while untitled young men, taule'ale'a, perform service, tautua, for their families and chiefs.
Fa'a Samoa is legally recognised in Samoa in areas such as village governance and customary land, and it is negotiated differently by Samoans abroad.
exampleEn: At a family funeral in Apia, mats are exchanged, the 'ava bowl is prepared, and young men serve food and carry water while the matai speak in order of rank.
qualificationEn: Practice differs between Samoa and American Samoa and between families, and the concept can be romanticised by outsiders.

titleEn: The kava circle: rank, roots and quiet talk
facts: Kava is a drink made from the pounded root of Piper methysticum, a pepper-family plant whose kavalactones have mild sedative and numbing effects.
In Tonga the formal kava circle, faikava, places the tano'a bowl in the centre, with a tou'a server and matāpule attendants, and the order of serving reflects rank.
In Fiji, yaqona is central to village welcomes; in Samoa, the 'ava ceremony marks formal occasions, with a high chief's cup served first.
Sessions often run late into the night with guitar music and conversation, and in Tonga the kava circle is a social institution where news and politics are discussed.
Kava is a legal social drink across the Pacific and an export crop, while concentrated extracts have raised liver-safety concerns in some markets.
exampleEn: In a Tongan village hall, men sit in a circle around the tano'a, clap once before drinking, and pass the cup in rank order while a guitar plays in the corner.
qualificationEn: Protocols differ between Tonga, Fiji and Samoa, and the kava circle is not a single regional institution.

titleEn: The Kula ring: gifts that must keep moving
facts: The Kula ring is a ceremonial exchange system among the Massim people of Milne Bay Province, Papua New Guinea, described by Bronisław Malinowski in Argonauts of the Western Pacific in 1922.
Two kinds of valuables travel in opposite directions between islands: soulava, red shell necklaces, move clockwise, and mwali, white shell armbands, move counter-clockwise.
A kula voyage involves canoe building, magic, and gift partners called karayta'u; the valuables are not money but carry histories and reputations.
Objects are held only temporarily before being passed on, and partnerships built through kula last for decades and support ordinary trade in food and pottery.
The system persists alongside the market economy and tourism, and Malinowski's account has been critiqued and refined by later anthropologists.
exampleEn: A canoe crew from one island arrives with a shell necklace, presents it to a partner, receives an armband in return, and the necklace begins its next leg the following season.
qualificationEn: The Kula ring covers many islands with different languages and practices, and the model is a simplification of varied local exchanges.

titleEn: Land diving: a leap that brings the yams
facts: Land diving, naghol, is a ritual performed on Pentecost Island, Vanuatu, between April and June after the yam harvest.
Men and boys jump from wooden towers roughly twenty to thirty metres high with liana vines tied to their ankles, aiming to land close enough for their hair to touch the ground.
The ritual is tied to the legend of a woman who escaped her husband by climbing a tree and jumping, and the vines caught her; it also serves as a harvest thanksgiving and a male rite of passage.
Villagers build the tower from trees and vines without modern materials, and divers observe preparation and taboo periods before jumping.
It inspired commercial bungee jumping, and it is now a major tourist draw, with only some villages performing for visitors.
exampleEn: On a hillside cleared for the tower, a young man climbs the platform, greets the crowd, and jumps as the vines snap taut and his shoulders brush the earth.
qualificationEn: The ritual belongs to particular villages on Pentecost with local rules, and tourism has changed its timing and staging.
